Sunflower microgreens on the moon: Growth evaluation in simulated lunar regolith 
and terrestrial soil mixtures under different irrigation levels. 
 
Team Name: Club la ciencia es divertida 
 
 
 
Team ID: 20444 
Team Members: Catarina M. Aponte Guzmán, Penélope M. Aponte Guzmán, Liem R. Jiménez Fernández, 
Dereck X. Negrón Ortiz and Karolina Z. Rodríguez Camacho 
Registered Coach: Lorna Ortiz Santiago 
 
Background 
Our project involved cultivating Helianthus annuus, Organic Black Oil Sunflower microgreens using a mixture 
of lunar regolith and soils. Microgreens are the early growth stage of certain edible plants, typically between 7 
and 14 days after germination. They are harvested while they are still young and are highly valued because they 
concentrate a large amount of nutrients. Microgreens are also easy to grow in small spaces and under controlled 
conditions. They are an excellent source of vitamin E, antioxidants, and healthy fats that benefit people’s heart 
and skin. They grow quickly compared to other plants; microgreens can be ready in less than three weeks, 
which is ideal for a moon mission where time and resources are limited. Microgreens need less water and space 
than fully developed plants, making them perfect for cultivation in resource-limited environments like the 
Moon. 
Hypothesis 
The higher the percentage of soil, the better the growth of sunflower microgreens. 
Independent Variable 
The amount of regolith and soil in the container for sunflower microgreens. 
Dependent Variables 
Average Height (in cm) and Humidity levels. 
Experimental measurements after the experiment concluded 
Average height of black sunflower microgreens, measured in cm. 
Controls 
The container used to plant the seeds, the regolith and soil mixtures, and the instruments. Also, the way we 
measured the ambient temperature, humidity, and microgreen height. 
Experimental Design 
We started our project on February 4th. We planted the seeds in 12 4oz plastic containers, divided into four 
groups, each one consisting of 3 containers. Two of the groups were for our Control Compositions of 100% Soil 
and 100% Regolith. The other two groups were for our Experimental Compositions of 75% Regolith + 25% 
Soil, and the 50% Regolith + 50% Soil. The experiment lasted for six weeks, during which we examined and

evaluated the development and growth of the microgreens, making adjustments as we considered would help us 
achieve better results. Due to the short period of cultivation of the chosen microgreens, we were able to adjust 
our experiment a total of two times. The Adjustment Report is shown in Appendix 1. 
Materials 
Seeds (Helianthus annuus, Organic Black Oil Sunflower) 
 
Lunar Regolith 
Soil for planting: Terra Mix Organic Seedling Mix 
 
Filtrated water 
Ruler to measure microgreen growth 
 
 
 
Spray bottle for water 
4oz plastic containers for planting 
 
 
 
 
Cellphone for pictures 
Digital Thermometer (Acurite) 
 
 
 
 
Humidity Meter (Soil Master) 
Humidity Meter (Soil master) 
 
 
 
 
30ml cup for watering 
Procedure 
(1) Prepare the mixture of soil and regolith for our experiment. Based on our variables, it will be 50% of each 
and a second one with 75% regolith and 25% soil. (2) Add up to 30ml water. (3) Soak the seeds the night 
before. (4) Drain and rinse the seeds on planting day. (5) Place (plant) 5 seeds on top of each container. (6) 
Cover for 4 days or until the microgreens lift the cover. (7) Record and verify the moisture of the soil and 
temperature daily. (8) Add water if needed; 10ml (when the humidity meter is red). (9) Expose to indirect 
sunlight to generate chlorophyll. (10) Harvest when ready (approximately 7 to 12 days). The sunflower 
microgreens will have the cotyledons. 
Results 
We observed that most seeds began to germinate on day 4. For the 100% soil variable all three phases went 
well, but mostly with the 10ml irrigation when the average growth was higher. The seeds were more resilient 
and grew more on the experiment's First Phase with the 10ml irrigation. See Appendices 2 through 4. 
Conclusion 
We conclude that the optimal experiment was the first one since the sunflower microgreens developed the best. 
Our hypothesis was supported by the data: “the higher the percentage of Earth soil, the better the growth of 
sunflower microgreens.” However, it was both surprising and educational to observe that the sunflower 
microgreens grown in 100% regolith grew in a very similar way to those planted in soil. This led us to 
investigate further into the properties of lunar regolith and the sunflower plant. 
With this knowledge, we can say that astronauts, by growing sunflower microgreens in a controlled 
environment, would have an excellent source of nutrition (including all the essential amino acids for the human 
body) and the ability to detoxify or decontaminate lunar soil. Based on our experiment and its results, we advise 
astronauts to plant sunflower crops multiple times in lunar soil before using it to grow sunflower microgreens or 
other microgreens and plants. We also recommend not only growing sunflower microgreens, but also setting 
aside some sunflowers to grow to full maturity and produce seeds to continue sunflower cultivation. For a more 
detailed Conclusion Report and Future Projections, see Appendix 5 and Appendix 6 respectively.

Appendix 4 
Graphs 
 
Humidity Legend: 0 – 24 Red (dry); 25 – 74 Green (normal); 75 – 100 Blue (excess) 
We observed that in all plantings the humidity was normal and good for the sunflower microgreen growth. Now 
the 100% Regolith and the 75% Regolith 25% Soil and 50% Regolith 50% Soil had a lot of humidity because 
the Regolith can “adsorb” water which means that the little water particles get retained on top of the fine 
Regolith particles which as a result the Regolith stays more humid. 
 
The average height of a microgreen is about ~6.3 cm. We observed that the 100% Soil sunflower microgreens 
were the ones that got close to the average of ~6.3 then followed by 100% Regolith. However, the ideal moment 
for harvesting a microgreen is when their two cotyledons are wide open; and in all the four plantings, most of 
the microgreens all had their two cotyledons open ready for harvest.

For this experiment, the planting and growing season, the temperature was about 81.3 F degrees. 
 
 
Humidity Legend: 0 – 24 Red (dry); 25 – 74 Green (normal); 75 – 100 Blue (excess) 
We observed that in the third experiment (the one with the most water being fed to the microgreens [15ml]) the 
humidity was higher, especially on the 100% Regolith and 75% Regolith 25% Soil.

We observed that in general the 100% Soil were the microgreens that grew tallest in all experiments, but also, 
we saw good growth in the other microgreens plantings as well. 
 
We can see that in the second and third experiments the temperature was the highest compared to the first 
experiment but still was under the same range of temperature.

Appendix 5 
Conclusion 
From our three experiments (each lasting 12 days) planting sunflower microgreens in 100% Earth soil, 100% 
Regolith, 75% Regolith 25% Earth soil, and 50% Earth soil 50% Regolith—with 10ml of irrigation water in the 
first experiment, 5ml in the second, and 15ml in the third—we found that our best experiment was the first one. 
This was because the amount of water was appropriate, and it was the one in which the sunflower microgreens 
developed the best. 
The sunflower microgreens that grew best were those in 100% Earth soil, followed by those in 100% Regolith. 
This is because Earth soil contains nutrients and has good water absorption, and in the case of lunar regolith, 
despite its low cohesion, it has good water adsorption, which allows the microgreens to grow properly and 
upright. One of the reasons why the microgreens in the 75% Regolith and 25% Soil mix, as well as the 50% 
Regolith and 50% Soil mix, did not grow as well could be due to chemical interactions between the regolith and 
soil that may have immobilized key nutrients, reducing the effectiveness of fertilization. Additionally, mixing 
lunar regolith with soil might have created a less chemically stable environment. On the other hand, the smaller 
soil particles could have blocked the pores in the regolith, affecting the roots’ ability to absorb water and 
oxygen. 
Our hypothesis was supported by the data: “the higher the percentage of Earth soil, the better the growth of 
sunflower microgreens.” However, it was both surprising and educational to observe that the sunflower 
microgreens grown in 100% regolith grew in a very similar way to those planted in soil. This led us to 
investigate further into the properties of lunar regolith and the sunflower plant. We discovered that regolith does 
not retain water internally, but its surface can adsorb water molecules, forming a thin film that allows the 
sunflower microgreens to have enough moisture to grow. So, even though regolith cannot absorb water due to 
its low cohesion, it can adsorb it, which keeps it fairly moist and suitable for the healthy growth of sunflower 
microgreens. We learned that absorption is when water penetrates into a material (like in sponges or clays), and 
adsorption is when water sticks only to the surface of the material without entering it. It's fascinating to know 
how lunar regolith does not absorb water, but it can adsorb it in a very thin layer on the surface of its particles. 
On the other hand, while researching the sunflower plant, we were amazed by the sunflower’s phytoremediation 
abilities—its capacity to detoxify soils from heavy metals and radiation, as happened in Chernobyl and 
Fukushima, where sunflowers were planted after the nuclear accidents! We learned what phytoremediation is 
and how this characteristic of sunflowers was a key factor in their healthy growth in 100% regolith. 
With this knowledge, we can say that astronauts, by growing sunflower microgreens in a controlled 
environment, would have an excellent source of nutrition (including all the essential amino acids for the human 
body) and the ability to detoxify or decontaminate lunar soil. Based on our experiment and its results, we advise 
astronauts to plant sunflower crops multiple times in lunar soil before using it to grow sunflower microgreens or 
other microgreens and plants. We also recommend not only growing sunflower microgreens, but also setting 
aside some sunflowers to grow to full maturity and produce seeds to continue sunflower cultivation. 
It has been a wonderful experience filled with many challenges and great learning. Thank you for the 
opportunity!

Appendix 6 
Future Projections 
 
For future experiments, we could consider testing how much sunflowers can detoxify and decontaminate lunar 
regolith by measuring which contaminants the sunflower absorbed and whether the regolith is truly fully 
detoxified afterward. This would allow us to assess how viable the seeds from sunflowers grown in lunar 
regolith are—whether the regolith still contains the proper nutrients to replant them as sunflower microgreens, 
and if they are suitable for human consumption.
